content.value_statement: Python HTTP clients need clear patterns for sync, async, streaming, and authentication. This skill provides focused HTTPX examples for common API workflows.
actual_capabilities: Shows basic HTTPX GET and POST request patterns.
Demonstrates synchronous and asynchronous HTTPX clients.
Provides examples for authentication headers and custom auth classes.
Covers streaming downloads, uploads, progress tracking, and retries.
Includes reusable sync and async API client class examples.
Lists optional packages for HTTP/2, WebSocket support, progress bars, and async runtimes.
limitations: It is documentation only and does not execute HTTP requests by itself.
It uses placeholder API URLs and placeholder credentials in examples.
It does not validate user-specific API schemas or authentication rules.
It does not provide automated tests for the example client classes.

use_cases.title: Prototype API Requests
use_cases.description: Quickly draft HTTPX GET, POST, timeout, and error handling patterns for a new Python integration.

use_cases.title: Modernize Async Services
use_cases.description: Convert blocking request patterns into async HTTPX clients with connection reuse and streaming support.

use_cases.title: Teach HTTP Client Patterns
use_cases.description: Use concise examples to explain authentication, retries, downloads, uploads, and reusable client classes.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Request
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to show a simple HTTPX GET request with status handling and a short explanation.

prompt_templates.title: Add Authentication
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to design an HTTPX client that sends a bearer token from a safe configuration source.

prompt_templates.title: Build an Async Client
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to create an async HTTPX client pattern with connection pooling, timeouts, and clean shutdown.

prompt_templates.title: Review a Production Workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to review my HTTPX workflow for retries, streaming, timeout settings, authentication, and error handling.

output_examples.input: Build a small HTTPX example for a GET request.
output_examples.output: A short Python-oriented explanation with request setup, status checking, response parsing, and common failure cases.

output_examples.input: Design an authenticated API client with HTTPX.
output_examples.output: A reusable client outline that covers base URLs, authorization headers, timeouts, request methods, and cleanup.

output_examples.input: Explain streaming downloads with progress reporting.
output_examples.output: A step-by-step description of streaming response chunks to a file while tracking total transferred bytes.

best_practices: Use one long-lived client per service boundary to benefit from connection pooling.
Set explicit timeouts and handle HTTP status errors for every external request.
Load tokens and API keys from safe configuration sources instead of hardcoding them.
anti_patterns: Do not create a new client for every request in high-volume code paths.
Do not copy placeholder secrets into real applications.
Do not download files without checking destination paths and response status first.

faq.question: Does this skill make network requests automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides examples and guidance for writing HTTPX code.

faq.question: Can I use it with Claude, Codex, and Claude Code?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill declares support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Does it cover asynchronous HTTP requests?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes AsyncClient examples, async streaming, and reusable async client patterns.

faq.question: Does it include authentication examples?
faq.answer: Yes. It shows basic authentication, bearer headers, and custom authentication classes.

faq.question: Are the API keys in the examples real?
faq.answer: No. The examples use placeholders and should be replaced with secure configuration values.

faq.question: Does it replace the official HTTPX documentation?
faq.answer: No. It is a compact guide for common patterns and should be checked against project requirements.
